newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong mood swings festive on handover eve.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong mood swings festive on handover eve.

text.p: Drawn by glorious weather and a sense of history, mobs of residents and tourists swarmed Hong Kong's harbourfront on Sunday, snapping souvenir photographs on the eve of the territory's return to China.
The royal yacht Britannia and its escort frigate HMS Chatham were the favoured backdrops, the royal banners and other flags and signal pennants whipping in a stiff breeze.
Couples and families jostled for position along the pier before the ships, posing for pictures on Hong Kong's last colonial Sunday in 156 years.
"It's sad to see Hong Kong go, but it was bound to happen sooner or later," said 21-year old Andy Barron, from Britain, as he snapped the Chatham.
"It's a great time to be in Hong Kong but I'm planning to stay out of the way on the night of the handover. I think it's mostly the Chinese who will be celebrating."
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday in a harbourside ceremony expected to be seen by more than 100 million television viewers world wide.
Security was heavy at the major handover venues on Sunday with police, in their last few hours of operation under royal insignia, carefully checking credentials and inspecting sealed manhole covers.
Any British serviceman in uniform on Sunday was immediately dragooned into becoming an extra in someone else's photograph.
One British officer, handsome in his dress whites, finally had to beg off from a long, orderly line of young women who had formed up in the blistering heat to have their pictures taken with him.
"I hate to say no to any young woman but I'm on duty and I have things I must do," he said as he hustled from the Chatham to the Britannia.

Across the street at the Prince of Wales barracks, which will be home to the Chinese army from Tuesday, Private James Canning of the Black Watch regiment stood guard in his green and black kilt, a distinctive red yarn ball dangling from his beret.
The 18-year-old was being manhandled by Chinese grandmothers and Japanese tourists, all of whom wanted their pictures taken with him.
"You take picture with me, I bring you a copy tomorrow," said one elderly Chinese woman as she wrestled Canning into snapshot position.
"I bring tomorrow because next day you gone."
Squads of street-cleaners in blue uniforms and conical straw hats raised clouds of dust as they cleared up behind the crowds.
Adding to the city's carnival air were tens of thousands of Filipina maids blanketing the city's shady spots as they do every Sunday, their one day off.
British Union Jacks were flying over all official buildings and from the balconies of some proud expatriates' flats.

Also much in evidence, even trailing from antennae on some taxis, was Hong Kong's red flag with its Bauhinia blossom. A few Chinese flags fluttered ahead of time from some junks plying Victoria Harbour.
At the Cenotaph monument to world war dead, two young Chinese men from Shanghai taking photographs of each other were philosophical about the handover.
"I think of Hong Kong returning to China as a kind of joint venture which will make both places even more fantastic than they already are," said William Tai, 24, a communications technician.
"It is time for Britain to leave. China and the Chinese must make their own way now."
